opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Jason. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential and won't be linked to your name.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Yeah, fine. Honestly, you're asking the right guy. I watch this happen every week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, "handy tool"? Come sit in my call centre. The voice bots took three desks near me last month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Even if it stops here, it's already too late for jobs like mine. It doesn't need to get smarter to answer "where's my parcel".

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep my head down, hit my numbers, take the angry calls the bot can't handle. Pay a bit off the credit card if I can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Already anxious. This one isn't the future for me, it's now.

S0.say: Handy tool? The voice bots took three desks near me last month.
S0.think: It's already too late for jobs like his. AI doesn't need to get smarter to answer simple customer calls.
S0.do: Hits his numbers, takes the angry calls the bot can't handle and pays down his credit card where he can.
S0.feel: Already anxious. For him this is now, not the future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say slow for who? It's not slow in call centres.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Slow might buy me a couple of years. They'd keep a few of us for the hard calls. But there's nothing else in this town, so when it goes, it goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Look at an online course, maybe IT help desk. Keep living with my parents and throw everything at the debt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same knot in my stomach. Maybe a bit looser.

S1.say: Slow for who? It's not slow in call centres.
S1.think: Slow change might buy him a couple of years, but there's nothing else in his town when it goes.
S1.do: Looks at an online IT help desk course, stays with his parents and puts everything into the debt.
S1.feel: Same knot in his stomach, a little looser.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be online saying it straight: companies fire people to please shareholders, then politicians shout and do nothing. Tax the bots. Give people a basic income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My job's done. Office work with a script is the first thing to go. And the new AI jobs? They're not coming to my town, and they're not for people with a two-year degree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sign up for whatever unemployment help there is. Apply for jobs in the city an hour away. Get my parents to help me look at the debt, which I've been too ashamed to show them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said moving to the city. Is that realistic with the debt?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. Rent there would eat me alive. More likely I'd drive in every day and hope the car holds up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. Angry too. Mostly scared.

S2.say: Companies fire people to please shareholders while politicians shout. Tax the bots and give people a basic income.
S2.think: His job is done, and the new AI jobs won't come to his town or to people with a two-year degree.
S2.do: Signs up for unemployment help, applies for city jobs he'd have to drive to, and shows his parents the debt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to protests, probably. Share prices booming while people like me lose everything? That's the whole system telling you who it's for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be unemployed with debt in a town with no jobs. Physical work's still there, so maybe a warehouse, but even that's not in my town. I'd be thirty-something living in my childhood bedroom with no way out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Take any warehouse or delivery shift I can reach. Look into debt relief. Join a group pushing for a basic income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like drowning slowly.

S3.say: Share prices boom while people like me lose everything. That tells you who the system is for.
S3.think: He'd be unemployed, in debt, in a town with no jobs, living in his childhood bedroom.
S3.do: Takes any warehouse or delivery shift he can reach, looks into debt relief and joins a basic income campaign.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly? I'd say I told you so. People laughed when call centre guys complained. Now it's coming for the warehouses too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The warehouse shift was my lifeboat. Without it there's nothing. At least now it's so many people that something has to change. Or everything breaks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Push for a basic income, loud. Look at the army. Stay with my parents and hope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Past scared. Just angry and empty.

S4.say: I told you so. People laughed when call centre workers complained, and now it's the warehouses too.
S4.think: The warehouse shift was his lifeboat. With so many people hit, either something changes or everything breaks.
S4.do: Campaigns hard for a basic income, looks at the army and stays with his parents.
